patient.name: Terence Doyle
patient.complaint: Sudden severe pain and coldness in his right leg for 3 hours
background: Calf claudication at 100 yards for 2 years

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with a suddenly painful, pale, cold, pulseless leg (acute limb ischaemia), with intermittent claudication, DVT and sciatica as distractors. Complications after revascularisation (compartment syndrome) are asked as 'most likely cause'.

points: Terence, 71, woke from a nap with **sudden right leg pain**.
The leg feels **icy cold** and numb.
He has had calf pain on walking for 2 years.

steps.lead: A clot has formed **inside** one of Terence's leg arteries, blocking flow and starving the tissue below it of oxygen.
Terence has every classic risk factor: **atherosclerosis** (his claudication), smoking, diabetes and high cholesterol.

points: Right foot **white** and cold to the knee.
No right popliteal or foot pulses; right femoral pulse weak.
Reduced sensation over the foot; toe movement weak.
Left leg: weak pulses but warm.

steps.lead: Terence's vascular exam (absent pulses, cold limb) and neuro exam (reduced sensation, weakness) together point to an occluded artery.

steps.title: The 6 Ps of acute limb ischaemia
steps.caption: Paraesthesia and paralysis mean nerves and muscle are dying: the limb is threatened.

steps.lead: Terence has **all six Ps**. Numbness and weak toes are the late, sinister ones.

visual.title: Time since onset
visual.label: Terence 3 h
visual.caption: Tissue damage becomes irreversible after **around 6 hours** without revascularisation.

steps.text: The clock started when the pain started.

steps.title: Thrombosis in situ vs embolism
head: Thrombosis
Embolism
rows: AF, recent MI, no prior symptoms

steps.lead: If Terence is not revascularised he risks **amputation** or death. Even after the artery is opened, watch for **compartment syndrome**.

steps.text: Claudication is pain on walking, relieved by rest. A **sudden** pale, cold, pulseless leg is acute limb ischaemia, even in a known claudicant.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?' (CT angiography) and recognise that acute limb ischaemia is first a clinical diagnosis; ABPI and bloods only add support in a stable patient.

steps.q: What makes the diagnosis in the first few minutes?
steps.r: Acute limb ischaemia is a **clinical diagnosis**. Do not wait for imaging to start heparin and call vascular.

steps.lead: Terence's diagnosis is made at the bedside from the **6 Ps**.
To plan revascularisation the vascular team needs Terence's **CT angiogram**: it shows exactly where the artery is blocked.

points: CT angiogram: occlusion of the **right superficial femoral artery**.
Widespread calcified plaque in both legs.
Reconstitution of flow below the knee via collaterals.

steps.lead: Terence is stable, so an **ABPI** and bloods add support and a baseline.

steps.title: Bloods
steps.text: Raised CK and lactate show muscle is already suffering. Baseline potassium matters: reperfusion can release a surge.

visual.title: ABPI, right leg
visual.label: Terence 0.3
visual.caption: Very low ABPI fits an occluded artery. Calcified diabetic vessels can read falsely high.

steps.text: Do not delay heparin and the vascular referral to get a scan. Imaging plans the operation; the 6 Ps make the diagnosis.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?' (IV heparin, analgesia, oxygen, urgent vascular referral) and 'definitive management' (revascularisation: thrombectomy, thrombolysis or bypass).

steps.r: **IV heparin** stops the clot propagating. Analgesia and oxygen support him while vascular surgery is called.

steps.lead: Terence gets an **IV heparin** bolus and infusion, IV morphine and oxygen, and an **urgent vascular surgery** referral.
Terence's long diseased SFA occlusion is revascularised; options are **thrombectomy, thrombolysis or bypass**.

points: Taken to theatre at 5 hours: thrombectomy and femoro-popliteal bypass.
Foot pink, warm, Doppler signals present.
Six hours later: **calf tense**, agony on passive toe stretch.

visual.title: After revascularisation
visual.caption: Pain returning after reperfusion with rising potassium: **compartment syndrome** and reperfusion injury. Fasciotomy relieved it.

steps.lead: Terence's care follows NICE and Vascular Society guidance on acute limb ischaemia.

steps.text: Pain out of proportion after reperfusion, worse on passive stretch, is **compartment syndrome**. Pulses can still be present.
Long term: smoking cessation, antiplatelet and **high-dose statin**, diabetes control, and anticoagulation if a cardiac embolic source is found.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: plaque rupture as the trigger, why ischaemia becomes irreversible at around 6 hours, why reperfusion harms, and how heparin works (antithrombin III).

steps.lead: One of Terence's femoral plaques ruptured, exposing collagen and tissue factor; platelets and the coagulation cascade did the rest.

steps.title: From plaque to occlusion
nodes: Subendothelial collagen and tissue factor exposed

steps.lead: Terence reached theatre at 5 hours, inside the **6 hour** window before damage becomes irreversible.
Restoring flow washed oxidative products and inflammatory mediators into Terence's swollen calf: **reperfusion injury** and compartment syndrome.
Heparin did not dissolve Terence's clot; it **potentiated antithrombin III** to stop it growing while surgery was arranged.

steps.text: Heparin works through antithrombin III (inactivates thrombin and factor Xa). Thrombolysis (alteplase) actually breaks clot down by activating plasminogen.

mcq.q: Which is NOT one of the 6 Ps?
mcq.r: The 6 Ps: pain, pallor, pulselessness, paraesthesia, paralysis, perishingly cold. Oedema suggests DVT.

mcq.q: Which is a key risk factor for arterial thrombosis?
mcq.r: **Atherosclerosis**, smoking, diabetes and hyperlipidaemia. The others are venous risk factors.
**CT angiography** identifies the exact occlusion site.

mcq.q: How is acute limb ischaemia first diagnosed?
If the patient is stable, which bedside test adds support?
mcq.r: **ABPI** and bloods add support in a stable patient.

mcq.q: What is the immediate drug treatment?
mcq.r: **IV heparin**, with analgesia, oxygen and urgent vascular referral.

mcq.q: After roughly how long does ischaemic damage become irreversible?

mcq.r: Heparin **potentiates antithrombin III**, preventing clot propagation.

technique.stem: A 76 year old man has a 2 hour history of sudden severe pain in his left leg. For a year he has had calf pain after walking 150 yards that settles with rest. He smokes and has diabetes. The left leg is pale and cold below the knee, with no popliteal or foot pulses, and reduced sensation over the foot.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question about a painful leg: is it acute or chronic, arterial or venous?

clues: 2 hour history of sudden severe pain
steps.x: Sudden onset + pallor + cold + pulseless + paraesthesia: the **6 Ps**, on a background of claudication.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Thrombosis on diseased artery: **acute limb ischaemia**.

elim: DVT gives a warm, swollen leg with pulses present.
Claudication is his background, but it is exertional and relieved by rest.
Spinal stenosis gives exertional leg pain relieved by bending forward, with pulses.
Sciatica is shooting pain down the leg with a normal circulation.

steps.x: **A. Acute limb ischaemia.** Rule: sudden, pale, cold, pulseless = acute limb ischaemia, even in a claudicant.

technique.stem: A 69 year old woman has a 4 hour history of a painful, pale, cold right leg with absent foot pulses. She has been given IV heparin and analgesia and the vascular surgeons have been called. Her pulse rate is 88 bpm (regular) and BP 150/84 mmHg. They need to know the exact site of the occlusion.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?

steps.x: It asks for the **diagnostic** test that maps the occlusion.
Clinical acute limb ischaemia already treated; now the surgeons need anatomy.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **CT angiography**: gold standard, shows the exact occlusion site.

elim: ABPI supports the diagnosis but does not show where the block is.
D-dimer is non-specific and does not localise anything.
Plain X-ray does not show arteries.
Venous duplex looks for DVT.

steps.x: **B. CT angiography.** Diagnosis is clinical; CT angiography locates the occlusion.

technique.stem: A 73 year old man has a 3 hour history of a painful, pale, cold left leg. He has numbness of the foot and weak toe movements. Femoral pulse is weak and there are no pulses below it. His pulse rate is 94 bpm and BP 162/90 mmHg. He has a history of claudication.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: IV unfractionated heparin and urgent vascular referral
Oral clopidogrel and vascular clinic in 2 weeks

steps.x: Initial management of a threatened limb.
6 Ps with sensory and motor loss: limb threatened, inside the 6 hour window.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **IV heparin**, analgesia, oxygen, urgent vascular surgery.

elim: Compression stockings worsen arterial flow.
A 2-week clinic wait would lose the leg.
Prophylactic dose does not stop clot propagation.
Exercise is for stable claudication, not an acute occlusion.

steps.x: **B.** IV heparin now, vascular surgeons now.

technique.stem: A 70 year old man has a femoral thrombectomy 5 hours after the onset of acute limb ischaemia. Six hours later his calf is tense and very painful, especially on passive stretching of the toes. Foot pulses are present. His potassium has risen from 4.4 to 6.0 mmol/L.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his new symptoms?

steps.x: A mechanism question about something new after revascularisation.
Pulses present (artery open), tense painful calf, potassium released from muscle.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Restored flow releases oxidative products and inflammatory mediators: **reperfusion injury** and compartment syndrome.

elim: Distal emboli cause a pale, pulseless foot; pulses are present.
HIT occurs after 5–10 days, with falling platelets.
Wound infection takes days and gives fever and erythema.
Re-thrombosis would make the foot pale and pulseless again.

steps.x: **E. Reperfusion injury.** Treat compartment syndrome with fasciotomy.

practice.stem: A 79 year old woman has a 3 hour history of sudden pain and numbness in her right leg. She has claudication and type 2 diabetes. Her pulse rate is 86 bpm (regular), BP 154/82 mmHg. The right leg is white and cold from mid-calf, with no foot pulses and reduced light touch sensation. Calf is soft and not swollen.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Sudden pain, pallor, coldness, pulselessness and numbness are the 6 Ps of acute limb ischaemia. DVT gives a warm, swollen leg.

steps.x: Diagnosis of an acutely painful leg.
Pain, pallor, perishing cold, pulseless, paraesthesia: the **6 Ps**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Acute limb ischaemia** from arterial thrombosis.

elim: Cellulitis is hot, red and swollen.
DVT is warm and swollen with pulses.
Neuropathy is gradual, glove-and-stocking, with a warm foot.
Claudication is exertional, relieved by rest.

steps.x: **A. Acute limb ischaemia.**

practice.stem: A 66 year old man who smokes 30 cigarettes a day has had calf pain on walking 50 yards for 3 years. This morning his left leg suddenly became painful. On examination the left foot is cool and pale. He has peripheral arterial disease in both legs and a regular pulse of 80 bpm. An ECG shows sinus rhythm and an echocardiogram is normal.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of his acute symptoms?
o: Arterial embolism from the left atrium
practice.e: In a long-standing claudicant in sinus rhythm with a normal echo, acute limb ischaemia is most likely due to in-situ thrombosis on a ruptured atherosclerotic plaque. Embolism needs a source such as AF.

steps.x: A 'most likely cause' question: thrombosis or embolism?

clues: calf pain on walking 50 yards for 3 years
peripheral arterial disease in both legs
steps.x: Long-standing atherosclerosis, no embolic source.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Thrombosis on a ruptured atherosclerotic plaque**.

elim: An embolus needs AF or a mural thrombus; ECG and echo are normal.
Spasm is linked to drugs such as cocaine or ergots.
Compartment syndrome follows trauma or reperfusion.
Baker's cyst rupture mimics DVT: swollen calf, pulses present.

steps.x: **E.** Claudicant + sinus rhythm = thrombosis in situ.

practice.stem: A 74 year old woman has a 2 hour history of a painful, cold right leg. She has smoked for 50 years and has hyperlipidaemia. Her pulse rate is 90 bpm and BP 148/86 mmHg. The doctor suspects acute arterial occlusion of the right femoral artery.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination of the right leg?
o: No pulses distal to the femoral artery
practice.e: Arterial occlusion causes absent pulses distal to the block, with a cold, pale limb. Oedema and warmth suggest venous disease or infection.

steps.x: A 'most likely finding' question for an arterial occlusion.
Arterial block: no flow below it.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Absent pulses** distal to the occlusion.

elim: Bounding pulses mean good flow.
Hot red skin is cellulitis.
Pitting oedema is venous or cardiac.
Varicose veins are chronic venous disease.

steps.x: **C.** Pulselessness is one of the 6 Ps.

practice.stem: A 68 year old man has had femoral thrombectomy for acute limb ischaemia. Eight hours later he has severe, worsening calf pain not controlled by morphine and pain on passive dorsiflexion of the ankle. His pulse rate is 110 bpm and BP 136/78 mmHg. Foot pulses are palpable.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Pain out of proportion and on passive stretch after revascularisation, with rising potassium and CK, is compartment syndrome from reperfusion injury. Pulses do not exclude it.

steps.x: Diagnosis of a complication after revascularisation.
Pain out of proportion + pain on passive stretch + pulses present + rhabdomyolysis bloods.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Reperfusion swelling in a closed compartment: **compartment syndrome**.

elim: Cellulitis takes days, with fever and erythema.
DVT causes swelling but not pain on passive stretch with rising CK.
Graft occlusion would make the foot pulseless again.
Neuropathy is chronic and painless or burning, not this.

steps.x: **B. Compartment syndrome.** Emergency fasciotomy.

practice.stem: A 72 year old woman presents 14 hours after her left leg suddenly became painful and cold. She lives alone and could not reach the phone. The leg is mottled with fixed staining, there is no sensation below the knee, and she cannot move her ankle. The calf is hard. Her pulse rate is 104 bpm and BP 140/76 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely state of the limb?
practice.e: Beyond about 6 hours without revascularisation, fixed mottling, paralysis and a hard calf indicate irreversible ischaemia; amputation is likely.

steps.x: A severity question: can this leg be saved?
Past the 6 hour window with fixed mottling, anaesthesia, paralysis and rigid muscle.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Irreversible** acute limb ischaemia: amputation rather than revascularisation.

elim: Chronic critical ischaemia is rest pain over weeks, not a sudden event.
A marginally threatened limb has no motor loss.
Claudication is exertional pain only.
A viable limb has no sensory or motor loss.

steps.x: **B.** After around 6 hours, damage becomes irreversible.

practice.stem: A 64 year old man with diabetes, hypertension and a 40 pack year smoking history has a 1 hour history of sudden severe right leg pain while sitting. The right foot is pale and cold with no pulses. His pulse rate is 84 bpm (regular) and BP 160/94 mmHg. There is no calf swelling or tenderness.
practice.q: Which is the most likely underlying process?
o: Atherosclerotic plaque rupture with thrombus formation
Paradoxical embolus through a patent foramen ovale
practice.e: Arterial thrombosis usually follows rupture of an atherosclerotic plaque, exposing collagen and tissue factor and triggering platelets and coagulation. His risk factors are all atherosclerotic.

steps.x: A 'most likely cause' question about the underlying process.

clues: diabetes, hypertension and a 40 pack year smoking history
pale and cold with no pulses
steps.x: Pure atherosclerotic risk profile, sinus rhythm, arterial picture.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Plaque rupture** with thrombus on top.

elim: No features of cancer.
Paradoxical embolus needs a venous clot and a PFO.
Vasculitis gives systemic features and young patients.
Venous stasis causes DVT, not a pulseless leg.

steps.x: **A.** Plaque rupture → platelets + coagulation → occlusion.

practice.stem: A 70 year old man has a 3 hour history of a painful, pale, pulseless left leg. He has received IV heparin and the vascular surgeons are planning revascularisation. His pulse rate is 88 bpm and BP 152/86 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to identify the site of occlusion?
practice.e: CT angiography is the gold standard, identifying the exact site of arterial occlusion before revascularisation. Normal renal function makes contrast safe.

steps.x: Which test shows **where** the artery is blocked?
Clinical diagnosis made; surgeons need anatomy.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **CT angiography**.

elim: ABPI shows reduced flow but not the site.
D-dimer is non-specific.
Echo looks for an embolic source, not the occlusion.
Venous duplex is for DVT.

steps.x: **B. CT angiography.**

practice.stem: A 67 year old woman has acute pain and coldness of her right foot for 2 hours. She can move her toes and sensation is intact. She is stable, with a pulse rate of 78 bpm and BP 146/80 mmHg. Foot pulses are absent. While awaiting imaging, the team wants a bedside test to support the diagnosis.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate bedside investigation?
practice.e: In a stable patient, ABPI and bloods add support to the clinical diagnosis of arterial occlusion.

steps.x: A **bedside** supporting test in a stable patient.
Stable, likely arterial occlusion, awaiting CT.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **ABPI** with a handheld Doppler.

elim: Nerve studies are for neuropathy.
X-ray shows bone, not flow.
Tilt table tests are for syncope.
No wound to swab.

steps.x: **A. ABPI.** Stable = ABPI and bloods for extra support.

practice.stem: A 75 year old man has a 2 hour history of a painful, pale, cold right leg with absent pulses below the femoral. He has reduced sensation in his foot. His pulse rate is 96 bpm, BP 158/88 mmHg and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial drug treatment?
practice.e: Immediate IV heparin prevents propagation of the thrombus while urgent vascular referral is made, alongside analgesia and oxygen.

steps.x: Initial **drug** for acute limb ischaemia.
Threatened limb inside the window.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Immediate **IV heparin**.

elim: Aspirin alone does not stop clot propagation.
Cilostazol is for stable claudication.
Oral DOAC is not the acute treatment; IV heparin can be stopped quickly for surgery.
Prophylactic dose is too low.

steps.x: **C. IV heparin.**

practice.stem: A 71 year old woman with acute limb ischaemia of the left leg has been given IV heparin, morphine and oxygen. CT angiography shows an occluded left superficial femoral artery. Her foot has reduced sensation but she can move her toes. Her pulse rate is 84 bpm and BP 150/82 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
practice.e: The limb is threatened but salvageable, so definitive treatment is revascularisation: thrombectomy, thrombolysis or bypass. Amputation is for irreversible ischaemia.

steps.x: **Definitive** management of a salvageable limb.
Initial steps done; occlusion located; limb still viable.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Revascularise**.

elim: Amputation is for an irreversible limb.
Compression worsens arterial flow.
Exercise is for stable claudication.
Anticoagulation alone does not restore flow.

steps.x: **C. Revascularisation.**

practice.stem: A 69 year old man presents with a 3 hour history of a painful, pale left leg. Pulses are absent below the knee and sensation is reduced. His pulse rate is 92 bpm and BP 162/90 mmHg. He has been given IV heparin and morphine.
practice.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
practice.e: After IV heparin, analgesia and oxygen, acute limb ischaemia needs urgent vascular surgery referral for revascularisation within the 6 hour window.

steps.x: Next step after heparin and analgesia.
Threatened limb, the clock is running.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Urgent vascular surgery** referral.

elim: Discharge would lose the limb.
Elective clinic is weeks away.
Outpatient imaging delays treatment.
A week is far beyond the window.

steps.x: **E.** Heparin + urgent vascular referral, then revascularise.

practice.stem: A 73 year old woman with acute limb ischaemia from a femoral artery thrombus is started on an IV unfractionated heparin infusion while awaiting thrombectomy. Her pulse rate is 88 bpm and BP 148/80 mmHg. A student asks how the drug helps.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of action of this drug?
o: Activates plasminogen to dissolve the clot
Inhibits vitamin K-dependent clotting factor synthesis
Potentiates antithrombin III to prevent clot propagation
practice.e: Heparin potentiates antithrombin III, inactivating thrombin and factor Xa, which prevents further thrombus propagation and buys time for revascularisation. It does not dissolve clot.

steps.x: A drug mechanism question: what does heparin do?
Monitored by APTT; given as a bridge to surgery.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Potentiates antithrombin III**, preventing propagation.

elim: That is alteplase (thrombolysis).
That is clopidogrel.
That is warfarin.
That is aspirin.

steps.x: **E.** Heparin stops the clot growing; it does not break it down.

prompts.q: What is arterial thrombosis and what are its risk factors?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: atherosclerotic risk profile points to thrombosis in situ.

points.p: Thrombus within an artery causing obstruction and downstream ischaemia
points.why: Arterial, not venous: pale and cold, not swollen.
Venous risk factors (flights, OCP) are distractors.

prompts.q: List the 6 Ps of acute limb ischaemia.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: paraesthesia and paralysis mean a threatened limb.

prompts.q: What do vascular and neurological examination show?

points.why: Pulses present suggests DVT or neuropathy instead.
Sensory and motor loss = threatened limb.

prompts.q: What are the complications if untreated and after revascularisation?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: before and after the operation.

points.p: Untreated: critical limb ischaemia, limb loss/amputation, death

points.why: Pain on passive stretch; pulses may be present.

points.p: Reperfusion injury from oxidative stress and inflammatory mediators

prompts.q: How is arterial thrombosis diagnosed and what is the gold-standard investigation?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: clinical first, imaging to plan.

points.p: First-line: clinical diagnosis from the 6 Ps
points.why: Do not delay heparin for a scan.

points.p: Gold standard: CT angiography, shows exact occlusion site
If stable: ABPI and bloods for support

prompts.q: What is the immediate management of acute limb ischaemia?
What are the definitive treatment options?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: revascularise unless the limb is dead.

prompts.q: What triggers arterial thrombosis and why is time critical?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: plaque rupture and the 6 hour clock.

points.p: Rupture of an atherosclerotic plaque exposing collagen/tissue factor
Platelet aggregation and coagulation cascade form occlusive thrombus

prompts.q: Why does reperfusion cause harm, and how does heparin help?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: what restored flow releases; what heparin binds.

points.p: Reperfusion releases oxidative stress products and inflammatory mediators

points.why: Prevents propagation, buys time; it does not lyse clot.

glossary.Acute limb ischaemia: Sudden loss of blood supply to a limb that threatens its survival.
glossary.6 Ps: Pain, pallor, pulselessness, paraesthesia, paralysis, perishingly cold: signs of acute limb ischaemia.
glossary.Pallor: Abnormal paleness of the skin from lack of blood flow.
glossary.Paraesthesia: Pins and needles or numbness from nerve ischaemia.
glossary.Paralysis: Loss of movement; in limb ischaemia it means muscle is dying.
glossary.Thrombus: A blood clot formed within a vessel.
glossary.Embolus: Material, usually clot, that travels in the blood and blocks a vessel elsewhere.
glossary.Atherosclerosis: Build-up of fatty, fibrous plaque in artery walls.
glossary.Plaque rupture: Breakdown of a plaque's cap, exposing material that triggers clotting.
glossary.Tissue factor: A protein exposed in damaged vessel walls that starts the coagulation cascade.
glossary.Subendothelial collagen: Collagen under the vessel lining; when exposed it makes platelets stick.
glossary.Coagulation cascade: Chain of clotting factor reactions ending in fibrin formation.
glossary.Claudication: Cramping leg pain on walking a set distance, relieved by rest.
glossary.Critical limb ischaemia: Severe chronic ischaemia with rest pain, ulcers or gangrene.
glossary.Compartment syndrome: Raised pressure in a closed muscle compartment cutting off blood supply; pain on passive stretch.
glossary.Fasciotomy: Surgical cutting of the fascia to relieve compartment syndrome.
glossary.Reperfusion injury: Tissue damage caused when blood returns to ischaemic tissue, releasing oxidative and inflammatory products.
glossary.Rhabdomyolysis: Muscle breakdown releasing CK, potassium and myoglobin.
glossary.CK: Creatine kinase; a muscle enzyme that rises when muscle is damaged.
glossary.CT angiography: Contrast CT of the arteries; gold standard for locating the occlusion.
glossary.ABPI: Ankle-brachial pressure index: ankle systolic pressure divided by arm systolic pressure.
glossary.Heparin: Anticoagulant that potentiates antithrombin III; given IV immediately in acute limb ischaemia.
glossary.Antithrombin III: A natural anticoagulant that inactivates thrombin and factor Xa; heparin boosts it.
glossary.APTT: Activated partial thromboplastin time; used to monitor unfractionated heparin.
glossary.Thrombectomy: Removal of a clot from an artery, surgically or with a catheter.
glossary.Thrombolysis: Dissolving a clot with a drug such as alteplase.
glossary.Bypass surgery: Using a vein or graft to route blood around a blocked artery.
glossary.Revascularisation: Restoring blood flow to an ischaemic limb.
glossary.Superficial femoral artery: The main artery of the thigh; a common site of atherosclerotic occlusion.
glossary.DVT: Deep vein thrombosis: clot in a deep vein causing a warm, swollen leg.
